m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a Google Colab notebook and run a code cell in it.
  • Know when JupyterLab on your own computer is the better choice, and install it if so.
  • Run a version check that proves scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, and matplotlib all import.
  • Fix the four setup errors students hit most often.

In Week 1 you'll watch a model score 94% and then find out a do-nothing guess scores 63%. That moment only lands if it happens on your own screen, in your own notebook. So before the first class you need one thing working: a notebook that runs Python with four libraries installed, scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, and matplotlib.

The class uses Google Colab. It's free, it runs in a browser, and all four libraries come preinstalled, so most people are done in five minutes. If you'd rather work offline on your own Windows, Mac, or Linux computer, JupyterLab is a fine alternative, and the code is identical in both.

#Where your code actually runs

Colab looks like a document, but every time you run a cell, the code travels to a computer in a Google data center, runs there, and sends the output back. Your notebook file lives in your Google Drive. Knowing this split explains most Colab surprises later: the notebook survives when you close the tab, but the running machine (and anything stored only in its memory) does not.

#Option A: Google Colab (the class default)

Colab works the same on Windows, macOS, and Chromebooks, because everything happens in the browser.

  1. Sign in to a Google account in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. A personal Gmail account is the safest choice; some school accounts have Colab switched off by an administrator.
  2. Go to colab.research.google.com.
  3. In the Open notebook window that appears, click New notebook. If no window appears, use File → New notebook in Drive.
  4. Click the name at the top left (it starts as Untitled0.ipynb) and rename it c4t-setup.ipynb.
  5. Click into the gray code cell, type print("hello"), and press Shift + Enter.

The first run takes a few seconds while Colab connects you to a machine. When it's ready, the top right shows a green check with RAM and Disk bars, and hello appears under the cell.

💡 Tip

Every notebook you create this way saves itself into a folder called Colab Notebooks in your Google Drive. You can always get back to it from drive.google.com or from Colab's File → Open notebook.

#Option B: JupyterLab on your own computer

JupyterLab is the same kind of notebook, running on your own machine. Pick it if you have a Windows, Mac, or Linux computer you're allowed to install software on and you'd like to work without internet. It takes about 15 minutes, and you'll type a few commands in a terminal.

scikit-learn's current release needs Python 3.11 or newer, so check that first.

Windows

  1. Open PowerShell (press the Windows key and type PowerShell) and run py --version. If it prints Python 3.11 or higher, skip to step 3.
  2. Otherwise install Python from python.org/downloads. If the installer shows a checkbox called Add python.exe to PATH, tick it. Close and reopen PowerShell afterwards.
  3. Make a course folder and install everything:
  1. Start JupyterLab with py -m jupyter lab. Your browser opens at an address like http://localhost:8888/lab.

macOS

  1. Open Terminal (press Cmd + Space and type Terminal) and run python3 --version. If it prints Python 3.11 or higher, skip to step 3.
  2. Otherwise install the macOS package from python.org/downloads, then open a new Terminal window.
  3. Make a course folder and install everything:
  1. Start JupyterLab with python3 -m jupyter lab. Your browser opens at an address like http://localhost:8888/lab.

Linux

  1. Run python3 --version in a terminal and check for 3.11 or newer.
  2. Many Linux systems block installing into the system Python (you'd see externally-managed-environment), so make a virtual environment for the course:
  1. Start JupyterLab with jupyter lab. Next time, run source .venv/bin/activate inside c4t-ml first.

Chromebook

Use Colab (Option A). ChromeOS can run Linux apps, but school-managed Chromebooks usually block that, and Colab gives you the same notebook with nothing to install.

numpy installs on its own, because pandas and scikit-learn depend on it. Once JupyterLab opens, click the Python 3 (ipykernel) tile under Notebook in the Launcher tab, then right-click the new Untitled.ipynb in the file panel and rename it c4t-setup.ipynb.

⚠️ Watch out

Leave the terminal window open while you work, because closing it shuts JupyterLab down. And always start JupyterLab from inside your c4t-ml folder: it can only see files in the folder where it started and the folders below it, so starting it elsewhere makes your notebooks seem to vanish.

#Prove the toolkit is ready

In either tool, paste this into a code cell and press Shift + Enter:

That output came from the computer that built this page. Your version numbers will almost certainly differ, and that's fine. What matters is the last line. Everything in this class works on scikit-learn 1.2 or newer, and Colab ships a recent release.

Notice that the package is called scikit-learn when you install it but sklearn when you import it. That mismatch causes the second problem in the next section.

#The four problems you're most likely to hit

1. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sklearn'. The library isn't installed in the Python your notebook uses. Run %pip install scikit-learn pandas matplotlib in a notebook cell, then restart: in Colab use Runtime → Restart session; in JupyterLab use Kernel → Restart Kernel. The %pip form (with a percent sign) installs into the exact Python the notebook is running, which avoids the classic "I installed it but it still says missing" loop.

2. The 'sklearn' PyPI package is deprecated, use 'scikit-learn' rather than 'sklearn' for pip commands. You typed pip install sklearn. That old name now fails on purpose. Install scikit-learn and keep importing sklearn.

3. Colab says your organization doesn't allow it, or the page won't load. A school Google account with Colab turned off is the usual cause. Sign in with a personal Google account instead (Colab's profile icon, top right, lets you switch accounts), or ask your teacher before the first class.

4. 'py' is not recognized or python3: command not found. Python isn't installed, or the terminal was opened before the install finished. Close the terminal, open a new one, and try again. On Windows, if py still fails, try python --version, then rerun the installer and tick the PATH box.

#Colab or JupyterLab?

When in doubt, use Colab. Both tools read and write the same .ipynb format, so a notebook made in one opens in the other, and you can switch at any point in the term.

Google Colab JupyterLab
Install needed No Yes (Python + pip)
Works offline No Yes, once installed
Where notebooks live Google Drive Folders on your computer
Works on a Chromebook Yes Usually not
Session ends when idle Yes No

Once the version check prints its last line without an error, you're set. The next lesson loads a real dataset, draws a chart, and trains a model to prove the whole chain works together.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a notebook remembers variables between cells, and why run order matters.
  • Load a dataset that ships with scikit-learn into a pandas DataFrame.
  • Inspect data with shape, value_counts, and describe, and draw a scatter plot.
  • Train and score a model with a fixed random_state, and match the class's result.

A version check proves each library imports. It doesn't prove they work together, and that's where setups usually break: pandas loads the data, but matplotlib draws nothing; or the model trains, but your score doesn't match anyone else's. This lesson runs the exact chain you'll use every week, so any problem shows up now instead of in the middle of Week 1.

Open c4t-setup.ipynb from the last lesson, or make a fresh notebook. Put each code block below in its own cell and run it with Shift + Enter. Every block on this page shows the output it really produced when this page was built.

#A notebook remembers, in the order you ran things

A notebook is a list of cells plus a running Python process called the kernel. When a cell creates a variable, the kernel keeps it, so later cells can use it. That gives you two rules worth learning on day one:

  • Run order matters, not page order. The number in brackets beside a cell, like [4], records when it actually ran. If cell 3 uses df and you never ran cell 2, you get a NameError.
  • The last line of a cell shows itself. If a cell ends with a value such as df.head(), the notebook displays it as a table without print(). This class mostly uses print() so your output looks like the page.

#Cell 1: load a dataset

scikit-learn ships a few small datasets, so nothing needs downloading. The wine dataset holds chemical measurements of 178 wines from three growers in the same region of Italy.

as_frame=True hands you a pandas DataFrame instead of a bare numpy array, so columns have names. The shape (178, 14) means 178 rows (wines) and 14 columns: 13 measurements plus target, which holds the grower as 0, 1, or 2. The three classes aren't the same size. Keep that in mind; it's the whole story of Week 1.

#Cell 2: look before you model

Before training anything, look at the numbers. head() shows the first rows and describe() gives a summary of each column.

Compare the min and max rows. alcohol stays between about 11 and 15, while proline runs from under 300 to almost 1,700. Columns measured on wildly different scales will cause a real problem for one of the models in Week 1, and you'll fix it with scaling in Week 2.

#Cell 3: draw a chart

This proves matplotlib can draw inside your notebook. Each class gets its own color.

Class 1 (orange) sits in the lower left: less alcohol, paler color. Class 0 sits to the right, and class 2 climbs highest on color. When classes pull apart this clearly with only two features, a model should do well with all thirteen. If you see the chart in your notebook, matplotlib works.

#Cell 4: train and score a model

You've trained a model like this before; here it's a smoke test. If your number matches the one above, scikit-learn is working and your results will line up with the class's. The two random_state=0 arguments are what make that possible: the split shuffles rows randomly and the tree breaks ties randomly, and fixing the seed makes both the same on every computer. Whether this score is actually good is the question Week 1 answers.

#What a run-order mistake looks like

Suppose you restart the notebook (or Colab disconnects) and then run only a cell further down. The kernel has forgotten everything, so the first unknown name stops the cell:

Here tuned_model was never created, which is exactly what you'd see after a restart for a name that was created earlier. The fix is never to retype the variable; it's to rerun the cells above. In Colab that's Runtime → Run all; in JupyterLab, Run → Run All Cells.

#If something goes wrong

What you see What it usually means Fix
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sklearn' scikit-learn isn't installed in this kernel %pip install scikit-learn, then restart the kernel
NameError: name 'df' is not defined You skipped a cell, or the kernel restarted Run all cells from the top
No chart appears plt.show() is missing, or the cell errored before it Read the error first; then add plt.show()
A different test accuracy A random_state is missing, or a very old scikit-learn Copy the cell exactly; check your version

⚠️ Watch out

Don't fix a NameError by pasting the missing line into the cell that failed. It works once, but now your notebook only runs in one magic order. When in doubt, use Runtime → Restart session and run all in Colab (or Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells in JupyterLab), which is how anyone else will run your notebook.

#Proof it works

Before Week 1, take a screenshot showing your chart and your Test accuracy line, and keep it handy. If a cell failed and the table didn't fix it, bring the exact error to the first class. Copy the last line of the red error text; that line names the real problem.

What you'll learn

  • Describe what happens before, during, and after each weekly class.
  • Name notebooks so a term's worth of work stays in order.
  • Tell which Colab files survive a disconnect and which vanish, and save the second kind somewhere safe.
  • Back up a notebook three ways: Google Drive, GitHub, and a downloaded .ipynb.
  • Explain why your numbers can differ from the lesson's, and fix it.

The most common way to lose a week of work in this class has nothing to do with machine learning. It's writing a results file in Colab, closing the tab, and coming back to find the file gone. Or starting JupyterLab in the wrong folder and thinking a notebook was deleted. Ten minutes of habits now prevents both.

#How each week runs

The class meets live once a week for 1.5 hours, for six weeks, followed by a capstone project. Each week has three lessons on this site, and each has a job:

  1. Notes: the ideas, with short examples you can run. Read these before class, even quickly; class goes much better when the words aren't new.
  2. Code-along: one small project we build together during class. Type the code instead of pasting it. Typing is slower, and that's the point, because you notice every argument.
  3. Practice: exercises that get harder as they go, each with a hint and a solution. Try each one for real before opening its solution.

A typical session: a recap and your questions (about 10 minutes), the week's ideas on screen (about 25), the code-along (about 40), and starting the practice set with help on hand (about 15).

💡 Tip

When you're stuck in class, paste the last line of your error into the chat. "It doesn't work" can't be debugged. ValueError: Found input variables with inconsistent numbers of samples: [142, 36] usually can, within a minute: it says your X and y have different lengths.

#Name notebooks so they sort themselves

Use one notebook per lesson, with the week number first so they line up in order:

Start each notebook with a text cell saying what it is and the date. In Colab, click + Text; in JupyterLab, change a cell's type to Markdown. Three weeks from now you'll be glad you did.

#Which files survive a disconnect

Colab keeps two kinds of things in two different places. The notebook (your code, text, and the last outputs) autosaves to Google Drive. Files your code writes, like a CSV of results, land on the temporary disk of the Google machine running your session. That machine is deleted when the session ends, and its files go with it.

Here's a cell that writes a small results file. Run it, then open the folder icon in Colab's left sidebar and you'll see outputs/ appear.

exist_ok=True means running the cell a second time doesn't crash just because the folder already exists. Any later cell can read the file back:

In JupyterLab, that file sits next to your notebook on your own disk and stays there. In Colab, it's gone after a disconnect unless you do one of the things in the next section.

#Three ways to back up your work

#1. Google Drive (Colab)

Notebooks you create with New notebook or File → New notebook in Drive already live in My Drive → Colab Notebooks. If the title starts with Copy of, or you opened a notebook someone shared with you, use File → Save a copy in Drive so you own an editable version.

To make files your code writes survive too, mount Drive at the top of the notebook:

Colab asks you to approve access. After that, anything you save under /content/drive/MyDrive/ (for example /content/drive/MyDrive/c4t-ml/outputs/) is a real Drive file. This cell only works inside Colab.

#2. GitHub

GitHub keeps every version of your work and gives you a link to share for the capstone. From Colab, use File → Save a copy in GitHub, pick a repository, and write a short commit message. From JupyterLab, create a repository on github.com and use Add file → Upload files to drag in your .ipynb files. GitHub displays notebooks with their outputs, so a reader sees your charts without running anything.

#3. Download the .ipynb

The simplest backup works everywhere. In Colab: File → Download → Download .ipynb. In JupyterLab: right-click the file in the left panel and choose Download. The file holds your code, text, and last outputs, and it opens in either tool.

#Why your numbers might not match the lesson

Many steps in machine learning shuffle data randomly. Here's the same split-and-train code run with three different seeds, then three times with the same seed:

Leave out random_state and every run uses a fresh random seed, so your score drifts from run to run and from the lesson's. That's the cause of almost every "my number is slightly different" question. Copy every random_state= argument exactly, and your output will match the page.

#Fixes for common problems

"I installed it but it still says ModuleNotFoundError." Your pip installed into a different Python than the notebook's. Run %pip install scikit-learn pandas matplotlib inside a notebook cell, then restart the kernel.

"Colab disconnected and my variables are gone." Colab deletes idle machines, and every session has a maximum lifetime (up to 12 hours on the free tier). Your code is still in the notebook; only the kernel's memory was lost. Use Runtime → Run all to rebuild it.

"JupyterLab opened but my files aren't there." You started it from a different folder. Stop it (press Ctrl + C twice in the terminal), cd into c4t-ml, and start it again.

"A cell shows [*] and never finishes." It's still running or stuck. Use Runtime → Interrupt execution in Colab, or the square stop button in JupyterLab. If that fails, restart the kernel.

⚠️ Watch out

Never keep the only copy of an important result in Colab's session disk or in a variable's memory. If it took more than a minute to produce, save it to Drive or download it before you close the tab.

  • The notebook came back because it lives in Drive. The CSV was on the old session's disk, which was deleted.

  • Files your code writes go to the session machine unless you write under a mounted Drive path or download them.

B. Files your code writes go to the session machine unless you write under a mounted Drive path or download them.

2Your test accuracy is 0.911 but the lesson shows 0.933, with the same code. What's the most likely cause?

  • A different seed gives a different split, and on 45 test rows one or two different wines move accuracy by several points.

  • load_wine is bundled with scikit-learn and is the same everywhere.

Show answer

B. A different seed gives a different split, and on 45 test rows one or two different wines move accuracy by several points.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run the five-step workflow (load, split, fit, predict, evaluate) and say what each step protects against.
  • Explain why a model must be scored on rows it never trained on.
  • Use stratify=y and random_state and predict what each one changes.
  • Build DummyClassifier and DummyRegressor baselines and judge a model by its gap above them.

A classmate tells you their tumor classifier is 63% accurate. Is that good? On the breast cancer dataset that ships with scikit-learn, a "model" that ignores every measurement and always answers benign also scores about 63%. Their model might have learned nothing at all.

That's the question this week trains you to ask about every number: compared to what? A score means something only when it was measured on data the model never saw, and only next to the score you'd get with no learning at all.

#Five steps you'll repeat all term

You trained a model before this class. Here's that process written as five steps, each with one job:

Here are the five steps on the breast cancer data: 569 tumors, 30 measurements each, labeled 0 (malignant) or 1 (benign).

Compare the two rows of ten labels: the tree gets two of them wrong. Training accuracy comes out higher than test accuracy, which is normal, because the model has already seen the training rows. Only the test number estimates how the model will do on the next patient.

model.score(X, y) is a shortcut: for a classifier it computes exactly accuracy_score(y, model.predict(X)).

#The test set is a sealed exam

Here's the intuition. Scoring a model on its own training rows is like grading a student with the exact questions they studied: a perfect memorizer gets 100% and learns nothing about new questions. A decision tree with no depth limit is a perfect memorizer. Watch:

The unlimited tree grows until every training row sits in a leaf with its own label, so training accuracy is a flawless 1.0. On the test rows it does worse than the depth-3 tree. If you had only looked at training accuracy, you'd have picked the wrong model.

Now the precise version. The test set is a stand-in for the future, and it stays honest only if nothing about it influences the model:

  • Fit nothing on it. Not the model, and (from Week 2) not the scaler or imputer either.
  • Don't tune against it. If you keep adjusting the model until the test score looks good, the test set has quietly become training data. Week 4's cross-validation lets you compare choices without spending it.

The three train_test_split arguments you'll use every time:

  • test_size=0.25 holds out 25% of rows. Between 0.2 and 0.3 is typical for small datasets.
  • random_state=42 fixes the shuffle so the split is identical on every run and every computer. The number itself means nothing.
  • stratify=y keeps the class proportions the same in both halves. It deserves its own section.

#Stratify: a fair split, every time

train_test_split shuffles rows randomly. With a small test set, luck can hand it noticeably more or fewer of one class than the full dataset has. Let's measure how much, using 20 different seeds and a 10% test set (57 tumors):

Because the labels are 0s and 1s, y_te.mean() is the share of 1s (benign). The plain splits wander across a range more than 25 points wide, so one unlucky seed gives a test set where a model looks better or worse purely because of which tumors landed in it. All 20 stratified splits land on one single point, as close to the dashed line (the full dataset's rate) as 57 rows allow. (*_, y_te = ... keeps only the last of the four returned pieces.)

Use stratify=y for every classification split unless you have a reason not to. You can't stratify a regression target directly, since nearly every value is unique.

#Baselines: the score to beat

A baseline is the score you get with no real learning. If your model can't clearly beat it, the model isn't useful, however impressive the number looks.

scikit-learn's DummyClassifier builds baselines that fit, predict, and score exactly like real models, so they slot into any comparison:

most_frequent looks only at y_train, finds the most common class (benign), and predicts it for every row, ignoring X entirely. That alone earns 0.629. Against that, the tree's 0.944 is a real improvement: it cuts the error rate from about 37% to about 6%. That's how to describe a model: not "94% accurate," but "cuts errors by five-sixths compared with always guessing benign."

The strategies you'll use:

  • "most_frequent": always the most common training class. The usual minimum to beat.
  • "stratified": random guesses in proportion to the training classes.
  • "uniform": every class equally likely.
  • "constant" with constant=0: always the class you name.

#Regression gets a baseline too

For a numeric target, the do-nothing model predicts the training average for every row. DummyRegressor does exactly that. The diabetes dataset's target is a disease-progression score measured one year later:

Mean absolute error (MAE) is the average size of a miss, in the target's own units. Lower is better. The linear model's typical miss is about 24 points smaller than just guessing the average, and that difference is the number worth reporting.

#Mistakes that inflate your score

⚠️ Watch out

Accuracy without a baseline. When 95% of emails aren't spam, a filter that never flags anything is 95% accurate and useless. Print the baseline next to every score; it costs three lines.

  • Fitting on everything, then splitting. The test rows have already shaped the model, so the score is too optimistic.
  • Forgetting random_state. Your score changes on every run, so you can't tell whether an edit helped or the split just got luckier.
  • Comparing models on different splits. Two models scored on different test sets aren't in the same race. Split once, then reuse X_train and X_test for every candidate.
  • Shopping for a seed. Trying 20 seeds and reporting the best one is tuning on the test set, just with extra steps.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A spam filter scores 95% accuracy on a test set where 95% of emails aren't spam. What does that tell you about the filter?

  • 95% is exactly what "never flag anything" scores here, so the number alone proves nothing.

  • The baseline also scores 95%. The filter might be no better than doing nothing.

  • Accuracy counts all emails together; it doesn't say how much of the spam was caught.

Show answer

B. The baseline also scores 95%. The filter might be no better than doing nothing.

2An unlimited decision tree scores 1.000 on training data and 0.923 on test data. A depth-3 tree scores 0.977 and 0.944. Which do you report as better, and why?

  • Training accuracy rewards memorizing. A tree that memorizes every row always scores 1.0 there.

  • Only the test score estimates performance on new data, and there the shallower tree wins.

  • Averaging train and test mixes an honest number with a dishonest one.

Show answer

B. Only the test score estimates performance on new data, and there the shallower tree wins.

3When does stratify=y change your results the most?

  • With many rows and even classes, random splits already land close to the true proportions.

  • With few rows, luck can easily over- or under-fill the rare class in the test set.

  • You can't stratify a continuous target directly; it's a classification tool.

Show answer

B. With few rows, luck can easily over- or under-fill the rare class in the test set.

4You train your model on split seed 0 and your teammate's on seed 1. Yours scores 0.95, theirs 0.93. What can you conclude?

  • The test sets contain different rows, so part of the gap (or all of it) is luck of the split.

  • A fair comparison holds the data fixed and changes only the model.

  • Nothing here compares training and test scores, so there's no evidence about overfitting.

Show answer

B. A fair comparison holds the data fixed and changes only the model.

Key takeaways

  • Fit on training rows only, and treat the test set as a sealed exam you open once.
  • Training accuracy rewards memorizing; the test score is the honest one.
  • stratify=y keeps class proportions identical across the split, which matters most for small or imbalanced data.
  • Always report a baseline. DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent") and DummyRegressor(strategy="mean") are the usual minimums.
  • Describe a model by its gap over the best baseline, on the same split, with a fixed random_state.

  • DummyClassifier reference (opens in a new tab): all the baseline strategies, with examples.

What you'll learn

  • Split once and score every candidate, baselines included, on the identical test set.
  • Write one evaluate function and turn its results into a pandas leaderboard.
  • Measure each model by how far it beats the strongest baseline, and chart it.
  • Rerun the comparison over ten splits to see which conclusions are luck and which are solid.

"I got 93%" is a weak claim. "The tree beats the best do-nothing baseline by 53 points, and it still wins on every one of ten different splits" is a strong one. Today you build the notebook that lets you say the second sentence. It's a tool you'll keep reusing, because every comparison in this course starts the same way.

Here's the plan. Everything flows from a single split, so every model faces exactly the same exam:

The data is the wine dataset from setup week: 178 wines, 13 chemical measurements, 3 growers labeled 0, 1, and 2. Make a new notebook called w1-codealong-baseline.ipynb and put each step in its own cell.

#Step 1: Load, look at the target, and split once

normalize=True turns counts into shares. Class 1 is the largest at about 40%. So before running anything, predict this: "always guess class 1" should score close to 0.40. Predicting your baseline before you compute it is a great habit, because if the real number surprises you, something upstream is wrong.

The split happens once, before any model exists. Every candidate below uses these same four variables.

#Step 2: Write one evaluation function

Repeating fit and score by hand for five models invites copy-paste bugs, like scoring model B on model A's test set. A function makes every candidate go through identical steps:

It returns a dictionary instead of printing, because a list of dictionaries turns straight into a pandas table. Training accuracy comes along too: a big gap between train and test is an early warning of overfitting, which Week 4 studies properly.

#Step 3: Score five candidates

Three baselines and two real models:

Read it row by row:

What you'll learn

  • Explain the fit / transform pattern every scikit-learn preprocessor follows.
  • Fill blanks with SimpleImputer and choose between mean, median, and most-frequent.
  • One-hot encode a text column, and handle a category that never appeared in training.
  • Scale features with StandardScaler and say which models need it.
  • Combine all of it in a ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline, and explain why that prevents leakage.

Hand LogisticRegression a single blank cell and it crashes. Hand it the word "north" and it crashes again. Real data arrives with both, plus columns measured in units that differ by a factor of a thousand. This week you fix all three problems, and you learn the one rule that keeps the fixes honest:

Every preparation step learns from the training set only.

That rule sounds fussy. By the end of this page you'll see it turn a model that "scores 73%" on pure noise back into the coin flip it really is.

#A messy dataset to practice on

The bundled datasets are clean, so we'll dirty one on purpose: blank out some measurements and add a text column naming the clinic each scan came from. Run the cells on this page in order in one notebook.

df.isna().sum() counts blanks per column; make it the first thing you run on any new dataset. Notice the order: we split before fixing anything. That ordering is the whole point of this week.

Here's what happens if you skip preparation:

The error message even names the two standard fixes: impute, or drop the rows. Let's weigh them.

#Drop the rows, or fill the blanks?

df.dropna() would delete 63 of 569 rows, about 11% of the data, to fix blanks in three columns. Dropping is fine when very few rows are affected and the blanks happen at random. It's risky when they don't. If one clinic's scanner often fails to record texture, dropping those rows quietly removes that clinic's patients, and the model learns less about exactly the people it'll later see.

Filling, called imputing, keeps every row. Here's the intuition: replace each blank with a typical value for that column. Now the precise version, and the most important pattern in scikit-learn:

  • fit learns something from data (here, each column's median) and stores it in an attribute ending in _.
  • transform applies what was learned to any data, including rows it has never seen.

Test blanks get the training median. That mirrors real life: when a new patient arrives tomorrow, all you have is what you learned from past patients.

Pick the strategy by the column: "median" for numbers (safer than "mean" when outliers pull the average), "most_frequent" for categories, and "constant" with fill_value= for a fixed placeholder like "unknown".

#Turning categories into numbers

Models need numbers. Replacing north / south / east with 0 / 1 / 2 invents an order that doesn't exist: is east "twice" south? One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column instead:

south becomes [0, 0, 1]. west never appeared during fit, so with handle_unknown="ignore" it becomes all zeros instead of crashing. Always set this: sooner or later, a category will turn up at prediction time that training never saw. (sparse_output=False only makes the output printable; inside a pipeline you can leave it out.)

#Scaling: putting features on the same ruler

mean radius is around 14, mean texture around 19, and mean smoothness around 0.1. To a model that measures distances, a change of 1 in radius looks a hundred times bigger than the whole range of smoothness. StandardScaler fixes that by subtracting each column's training mean and dividing by its training standard deviation, so every feature ends up centered on 0 with a spread of 1:

Scaling matters for models that compare distances or weigh features against each other: k-NN, logistic regression, support vector machines, neural networks. Decision trees and random forests split on one feature at a time, so scale doesn't change them. (A printed -0.0 is just a rounding artifact.)

#One object for the whole recipe: ColumnTransformer + Pipeline

Different columns need different steps. ColumnTransformer routes each group of columns to its own steps, and Pipeline chains the preparation with the model:

One model.fit(X_train, y_train) call fits every imputer, scaler, and encoder on training rows, then trains the classifier on the result. One model.score(X_test, y_test) call transforms the test rows with what was learned and predicts. You can't accidentally fit on test data, because there's no place in this code where that could happen.

#Leakage: when the test set sneaks into training

Data leakage means information from the test rows influences training, so your test score beats what real life will give you. Here's the most dramatic version. The data below is pure noise: random features, random labels. The honest accuracy of any model is a coin flip.

Nothing real can be learned here, yet the leaky version reports 73%. Out of 5,000 noise columns, a few line up with the labels by pure chance, including on the test rows, and selecting on all 200 rows finds exactly those. The pipeline selects using training rows only and lands near 50%, the truth. (make_pipeline is a shortcut that names the steps for you.)

Fitting a scaler or imputer on all rows leaks the same way, just less dramatically. The fix never changes: split first, and put every fitted step inside the pipeline.

⚠️ Watch out

StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) on your full dataset, before train_test_split, is the most common leak in student projects. Whenever you see fit or fit_transform called on anything other than training data, stop and move that step into the pipeline.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A teammate runs X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) and then train_test_split. Their test score looks fine. What's the problem?

  • Leakage isn't about labels. The test rows helped set the mean and standard deviation the model trains with.

  • Any fit that sees test rows leaks. Put the scaler in a pipeline and fit it after the split.

  • Scaling prepares the features, so it always comes before the model.

Show answer

B. Any fit that sees test rows leaks. Put the scaler in a pipeline and fit it after the split.

2Which of these models gives the same predictions whether or not you scale the features?

  • k-NN measures distances, so a feature with big numbers dominates unless you scale.

  • Its regularization treats feature weights together, so scaling can change the fitted model.

  • A tree splits one feature at a time on a threshold. Rescaling moves the threshold but not which rows go where.

Show answer

C. A tree splits one feature at a time on a threshold. Rescaling moves the threshold but not which rows go where.

3An income column has a few huge values and 5% blanks. Which imputer strategy fits best?

  • A few huge incomes drag the mean far above what a typical person earns.

  • The median ignores how extreme the outliers are, so it fills blanks with a typical value.

  • For a continuous number nearly every value is unique, so "most frequent" is close to arbitrary.

Show answer

B. The median ignores how extreme the outliers are, so it fills blanks with a typical value.

4A new scan arrives from a clinic called "west", which never appeared in training. With OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), what happens?

  • That's what happens with the default handle_unknown="error".

  • The row simply doesn't match any known clinic, and the model relies on the other features.

  • An encoder's columns are fixed at fit time. Adding one would break the trained model.

Show answer

B. The row simply doesn't match any known clinic, and the model relies on the other features.

Key takeaways

  • Split first. Every preprocessor fits on training rows only and transforms everything else.
  • SimpleImputer fills blanks: median for skewed numbers, most frequent for categories.
  • OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") turns categories into 0/1 columns without crashing on new ones.
  • StandardScaler matters for distance- and weight-based models, not for trees.
  • A ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline makes leakage impossible by construction, and leakage can turn pure noise into a convincing score.

#Step 1: Make the data realistic

pd.cut sorts each number into a labeled bin, which gives us a text column to encode. We reuse last week's random_state=7 split so today's numbers compare directly with last week's leaderboard.

Before fixing anything, let's measure the problem. k-NN classifies a wine by finding the training wines closest to it, using straight-line distance across all features. For two random wines, each feature adds to that squared distance in proportion to its variance. So the share of total variance is the share of k-NN's attention each feature gets:

proline alone accounts for almost all of the distance. Twelve chemical measurements went in, and k-NN listens to one. After StandardScaler, every numeric column has variance 1, so each gets an equal 1/12 share. That's the hypothesis to test.

#Step 2: Build the pipeline, with and without scaling

A small function that builds the pipeline lets you flip one setting and compare fairly:

Same model, same data, same split. The only change is one StandardScaler, and accuracy jumps by more than 30 points. The hypothesis holds: k-NN was never a bad model for wine, it was asking the wrong question ("which wines have similar proline?").

Look at how the pieces fit:

  • Numeric columns go through impute, then scale, in that order. StandardScaler can't compute a mean over a column that still has NaN in it.
  • color has no blanks here, so it goes straight to OneHotEncoder. If it could have blanks, you'd put a most_frequent imputer in front of it, as in the Notes.
  • fit returns the pipeline itself, so build(...).fit(...) gives a trained pipeline in one line.

#Step 3: Predict on brand-new, messy rows

A pipeline earns its keep when new data arrives. Take two test wines, blank out one's proline, and give the other a color word training never saw:

Neither row crashes the model, and both predictions are correct. The blank proline is filled with the training median. The unknown "purple" becomes all zeros in the color columns, thanks to handle_unknown="ignore". You hand the pipeline raw data, and it repeats every preparation step exactly as it learned them during fit.

#Step 4: Swap in other models

The preparation half of the pipeline doesn't care which model comes after it. clone makes a fresh, unfitted copy of it, so each model gets its own:

k-NN (orange) went from the weakest real model last week to a tie with the tree. Logistic regression scored a perfect 1.000, but that's 45 out of 45 wines: one different split could easily make it 43 of 45. Don't crown a winner from one small test set; Week 4's cross-validation is the tool for that.

max_iter=1000 gives logistic regression more steps to settle on its answer. If you ever see a ConvergenceWarning, raise it, or check that your features are scaled.

⚠️ Watch out

Without clone, every pipeline in the loop would share one ColumnTransformer, and each fit would overwrite the medians and scales the previous one learned. Here they'd all learn the same numbers, so nothing visibly breaks, but shared fitted objects cause baffling bugs later. Clone, or build a fresh one each time.

#Exercise 4: A full mixed-type pipeline

Run this setup. It replaces wine's alcohol column with a text label and adds blanks to two columns:

Build a ColumnTransformer that imputes (median) and scales every numeric column, and imputes (most frequent) and one-hot encodes alcohol_level. Put it in a Pipeline with LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000). Print the test accuracy and the number of features the model receives after preprocessing.

Need a hint?

The numeric columns are Xw.columns.drop("alcohol_level").tolist(). Each branch can be a make_pipeline(...) of two steps. After fitting, model.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out() lists every output column.

Show solution

12 numeric columns plus 3 one-hot columns (low, mid, high) make 15. A perfect score on 45 test wines is great to see, but on a test set this small it's a single draw, not proof of a perfect model.

#Exercise 5: Is "missing" a clue?

Sometimes whether a value is blank tells you something. In this setup, texture readings go missing only for malignant tumors (label 0):

Split with test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0. Compare two pipelines of SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=flag), then StandardScaler(), then LogisticRegression(), with flag set to False and then True.

Need a hint?

Loop over [False, True] and build a fresh pipeline inside the loop. add_indicator=True appends one extra 0/1 column per feature that had blanks during fit.

Show solution

add_indicator=True adds a column meaning "this texture was blank." The model learns that a blank texture strongly suggests malignant, and accuracy climbs by several points. Real data does this all the time (a lab test gets ordered only for patients who already look sick). The catch: if the reason values go missing changes later, the clue quietly stops working.

#Exercise 6: The feature that knows the answer

A hospital export includes a column followup_visits: the number of oncology appointments booked for each patient. Run the setup, then train a scaled LogisticRegression on all four columns and print test accuracy. Next, score a model on each column alone. Which column is suspicious, and why must it be removed even though no fit ever touched the test set?

Need a hint?

For each column, ask one question: would I know this value at the moment I need the prediction? Follow-up appointments get booked after a diagnosis.

Show solution

followup_visits alone predicts almost as well as everything together. That's the red flag: one column that's nearly as good as the answer key. It is a consequence of the answer, recorded after doctors already knew the diagnosis, so at prediction time (a new scan, no diagnosis yet) it doesn't exist. This is target leakage, and a pipeline can't catch it, because nothing was fit on test rows; the leak is in what the column means. The honest model is the one without it.

#Challenge: How bad can leakage get?

Write leak_test(n_features, seed). It builds a pure-noise dataset (200 rows, n_features random columns, random 0/1 labels) and returns two test accuracies:

  • leaky: SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10) fit on all rows, then split (test_size=0.3, random_state=0), then LogisticRegression.
  • honest: split first, then a pipeline of the same two steps.

Average each over seeds 0 to 4 for n_features of 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000, and plot both lines. What pattern do you see, and why does the 10-feature case show no leak?

Need a hint?

np.mean([leak_test(n, s) for s in range(5)], axis=0) averages pairs of numbers column by column. With k=10 and only 10 features, ask yourself what SelectKBest actually selects.

Show solution

The honest score hovers near 50%, which is right for random labels. The leaky score climbs as features grow: the more noise columns there are to search, the more of them line up with the labels by chance, test rows included, and leaky selection finds exactly those. With only 10 features and k=10, selection keeps every column, so it chooses nothing and there's nothing to leak. Datasets with thousands of columns (genes, words, pixels) are where this mistake does the most damage.

What you'll learn

  • Build and read a confusion matrix, and name its four cells.
  • Compute precision, recall, and F1 by hand and with scikit-learn.
  • Explain what the decision threshold does, and predict what moving it changes.
  • Read a precision-recall curve and an ROC curve.
  • Pick the metric that fits a problem, based on what each mistake costs.

A tumor model that's 92% accurate sounds trustworthy until you ask about the other 8%. Telling a healthy patient they might have cancer means an extra scan and a frightening week. Telling a cancer patient they're fine can cost their life. Accuracy counts those two mistakes as equal.

This week you learn metrics that keep them apart, and the one dial, the decision threshold, that controls how many of each you make.

#A screening model to study

We'll build a deliberately simple model from just two measurements, tumor radius and texture, so it makes enough mistakes to be interesting. Run the cells on this page in order.

Why flip the labels? scikit-learn's metric functions treat label 1 as the positive class: the thing you're trying to detect. In this dataset, 1 originally meant benign. Flipping makes "positive" mean "malignant," which is what a screening test hunts for. Mixing up the positive class is one of the easiest ways to report the wrong numbers, so always check which class is 1.

#The confusion matrix: four kinds of outcome

Every prediction lands in one of four boxes:

  • True positive (TP): malignant, and the model said malignant.
  • True negative (TN): benign, and the model said benign.
  • False positive (FP): benign, but the model said malignant. A false alarm.
  • False negative (FN): malignant, but the model said benign. A missed cancer.

Here's how a program tallies them, one prediction at a time. Step through it and watch the four counters:

scikit-learn does the same tally for our 143 test tumors and arranges it in a 2×2 grid:

Rows are the true class and columns the predicted class, both in the order 0 then 1. The top row is the 90 benign tumors: 87 cleared, 3 false alarms. The bottom row is the 53 malignant ones: 45 caught, 8 missed. .ravel() flattens the grid in the order TN, FP, FN, TP, a sequence worth memorizing.

#Four metrics from four numbers

Here's the intuition first. Precision asks: when the model raises the alarm, how often is it right? Recall asks: of all the real cases, how many did the alarm catch? Now precisely:

  • Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all predictions.
  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP). High precision means few false alarms.
  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN). High recall means few misses. Also called sensitivity, or the true positive rate.
  • F1 = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall), the harmonic mean, which is high only when both are high.

The model rarely raises a false alarm, but it misses about one cancer in seven. That weakness was hiding inside "92% accurate."

Why a harmonic mean? Suppose precision were 1.0 and recall 0.02: the model flags one tumor, correctly, and misses the rest. The ordinary average is 0.51, which sounds passable. F1 is about 0.04, which is honest about how useless that model is.

classification_report prints all of this for both classes at once:

support is how many true examples each class has. Macro avg weights the two classes equally; weighted avg weights them by support, so the bigger class counts more.

#The decision threshold

predict hides a choice. Logistic regression really outputs a probability, and predict says "malignant" whenever that probability is at least 0.5. Nothing makes 0.5 special.

Get the probabilities yourself and try other cutoffs:

predict_proba returns one column per class, in the order of model.classes_ (here [0, 1]), so [:, 1] is the malignant column.

This is the precision-recall trade-off. Raise the threshold and the model flags only tumors it's very sure about: hardly any false alarms, but many missed cancers. Lower it and it catches nearly everything, but sends dozens of healthy patients for more tests. Plotting both metrics against every possible threshold shows the whole trade at a glance:

precision_recall_curve tries every distinct probability as a threshold. It returns one more precision and recall value than thresholds, which is why the plot drops the last one with [:-1].

No threshold is "correct." You choose one by what each mistake costs. For a first screening test, where a false alarm means one more scan, 0.3 or lower is reasonable. For a spam filter, where a false positive buries a real email, you'd go higher.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't choose a threshold by trying values on the test set and keeping the best. That tunes the model on test data, and the score you report will be too optimistic. Choose it on a separate validation split, then confirm it once on the test set. The code-along shows exactly how.

#Every threshold at once: PR and ROC curves

Sometimes you want to compare models before anyone has picked a threshold. Two curves do that by sweeping every threshold and plotting one point for each:

  • The precision-recall (PR) curve plots precision against recall. Its summary number is average precision (AP); higher is better.
  • The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN), the share of benign tumors wrongly flagged. Its summary is the area under the curve (ROC AUC): 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random guessing.

The legends show each curve's summary number. Both are handy for comparing models, but neither tells you which threshold to use: to put a model to work you still choose one point on the curve. When the positive class is rare, the PR curve is usually the more revealing of the two, because the ROC curve's false positive rate stays small when negatives vastly outnumber positives. Week 6 returns to that.

#Which metric for which job?

  • Recall when misses are expensive: disease screening, fraud detection, safety alerts.
  • Precision when false alarms are expensive: spam filtering, flagging someone for a costly treatment or a police stop.
  • F1 when you need one number that balances both, especially with a rare positive class.
  • Accuracy only when classes are roughly balanced and both mistakes cost about the same.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model flags 40 transactions as fraud. 30 really are fraud, and 20 other frauds went unflagged. What are its precision and recall?

  • Those are swapped. Precision divides by what was flagged; recall divides by what was real.

  • Precision = 30 / 40 flagged. Recall = 30 / (30 + 20) real frauds.

  • Recall's denominator is all 50 real frauds, not the 40 flagged.

Show answer

B. Precision = 30 / 40 flagged. Recall = 30 / (30 + 20) real frauds.

2You lower the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2. Which change should you expect?

  • More cases get flagged, so fewer real ones slip through, but more of the flags are false alarms.

  • Lowering the threshold can't remove a false alarm; it only adds flags.

  • Accuracy can rise or fall, depending on how many new false alarms the extra flags bring.

Show answer

A. More cases get flagged, so fewer real ones slip through, but more of the flags are false alarms.

3A school wants a model that flags essays for a plagiarism investigation, which is stressful and time-consuming for the student. Which metric should matter most?

  • Catching everything at the cost of accusing many honest students would do real harm here.

  • When a false alarm is costly to an innocent person, you want flags you can trust.

  • Most essays aren't plagiarized, so accuracy would mostly reward clearing everyone.

Show answer

B. When a false alarm is costly to an innocent person, you want flags you can trust.

4Your report says "recall 0.97" on the original breast cancer labels, where 1 means benign. What did you actually measure?

  • With 1 = benign, the positive class is benign, so recall counts benign tumors.

  • The default pos_label=1 points recall at whichever class is labeled 1. Flip the labels or pass pos_label=0.

  • Recall only needs predicted and true labels.

Show answer

B. The default pos_label=1 points recall at whichever class is labeled 1. Flip the labels or pass pos_label=0.

Key takeaways

  • A confusion matrix splits mistakes into false alarms (FP) and misses (FN); accuracy blends them together.
  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP) measures trust in a flag. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) measures coverage of real cases.
  • F1 is high only when both are high.
  • predict uses a 0.5 threshold on predict_proba. Moving it trades precision for recall, and the right setting depends on what each mistake costs.
  • PR and ROC curves summarize every threshold; you still have to pick one point to deploy, and you pick it on validation data.
  • Always confirm which class is labeled 1.

#Further reading

  • Accuracy, precision, and recall (opens in a new tab): Google's crash course, with interactive examples.
  • Thresholds and the confusion matrix (opens in a new tab): a widget that lets you drag a threshold and watch the four cells change.
  • Metrics and scoring (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's reference for every classification metric, including pos_label and averaging options.

What you'll learn

  • Split data three ways and say what each part is allowed to decide.
  • Build a threshold table that reports results in counts a business understands.
  • Turn a requirement ("catch at least 80% of fraud") into a threshold, using validation data only.
  • Confirm the choice once on the test set, and report an honest result when it falls short.
  • Package the threshold so it lives in one place.

A bank's fraud team gives you a rule: "We can review a few dozen flagged transactions a day. Catch at least 80% of fraud." That's a real requirement, and model.predict() with its built-in 0.5 cutoff knows nothing about it. Today you build the tool that turns a requirement like that into a threshold, and you see why the test set has to stay sealed while you choose it.

Here's the plan. The data gets split three ways, and each part has exactly one job:

The finished notebook ends with a function, flag_fraud, that applies your chosen threshold to new transactions, plus a test-set confusion matrix showing exactly how many frauds it catches and how many false alarms it costs. Create w3-codealong-threshold.ipynb and run the cells in order.

#Step 1: Three sets, not two

Choosing a threshold is a decision made from data, just like fitting a model. Make it on the test set and the test score stops being honest. So we carve out a validation set for decisions and keep the test set for the final check.

The second split takes 25% of the remaining 80%, which is 20% of the whole. Stratifying both times keeps fraud at about 10% in every part. make_classification builds a synthetic dataset: weights=[0.9, 0.1] sets the class balance, and class_sep=0.8 makes the classes overlap enough that the problem is genuinely hard.

#Step 2: Train, and check the default threshold

96% accuracy, and the fraud team would reject it. Class 1's recall is 0.645, so about one fraud in three gets through. Precision is excellent, meaning the model flags only when it's very confident. The default threshold puts this model on the wrong side of the trade-off for this job.

#Step 3: Build a threshold table

Instead of trying thresholds one at a time, write a function that scores a whole range at once:

Read down the table and you can watch the trade-off happen. As the threshold rises, false_alarms falls toward 0 while missed climbs. The caught, missed, and false_alarms columns are what you'd actually show the fraud team: they care about "33 extra reviews," not "precision 0.612."

zero_division=0 tells precision_score what to return when a threshold flags nothing at all and precision would be 0/0.

Nineteen rows of numbers are easier to read as a picture. The dashed line is the fraud team's requirement:

#Step 4: Turn the requirement into a threshold

The rule was "catch at least 80%." Among the thresholds that meet it, take the highest, because a higher threshold means fewer false alarms for the team to wade through:

On validation, 0.20 catches 52 of 62 frauds at the price of 33 false alarms. The F1-best threshold, 0.35, would be the pick if there were no business rule, but it misses 15 frauds, which breaks the requirement. The requirement decides the threshold; F1 is a fallback for when there isn't one.

#Step 5: Confirm once on the test set

Now, and only now, open the test set. Compare the default with the chosen threshold, as numbers and as two confusion matrices:

The chosen threshold catches 10 more frauds than the default. But test recall is 0.726, below the 0.80 we saw on validation. That isn't a bug. With only 62 frauds in each set, a handful of borderline transactions moves recall by several points, and the validation set happened to be a little kind.

What you must not do is lower the threshold again until the test set says 0.80. That turns the test set into a second validation set, and you'd have no honest number left. Report what happened instead: "At threshold 0.2 the model caught 73% of fraud on held-out data and 84% on validation, so expect recall somewhere in that range." Then shrink the uncertainty with more data, or with Week 4's cross-validation, which averages over many validation splits instead of trusting one.

#Step 6: Package it

The last number is precision, in words the team understands: about half the reviews will turn out to be real fraud. The threshold now lives in one place, so changing it later means editing one value.

⚠️ Watch out

A threshold belongs to one specific trained model. Retrain it, even on the same data with different settings, and the probabilities shift. Choose the threshold again on validation data every time.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the threshold get chosen on the validation set rather than the test set?

  • Here they're the same size. The difference is what each set is allowed to influence.

  • The test set stays untouched until the decision is final, so its score is a fair preview of real use.

  • predict_proba works on any rows; the issue is which rows influence your decisions.

Show answer

B. The test set stays untouched until the decision is final, so its score is a fair preview of real use.

2Thresholds 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 all meet the 80% recall target on validation. Why pick 0.20?

  • The best F1 was at 0.35, which fails the target. The rule here is about false alarms.

  • Each step down adds reviews without being required by the rule.

  • Lower thresholds flag more transactions, so recall goes up or stays the same.

Show answer

B. Each step down adds reviews without being required by the rule.

3Test recall comes out at 0.726, below the 0.80 target. What's the honest next step?

  • That tunes on the test set, and then the 0.80 is no longer an honest estimate.

  • A small validation set gave an optimistic estimate; the fix is better validation, not test-set tuning.

  • Then the test set is training data, and you have nothing left to evaluate with.

Show answer

B. A small validation set gave an optimistic estimate; the fix is better validation, not test-set tuning.

Key takeaways

  • Train fits the model, validation chooses settings like the threshold, and test confirms once.
  • A threshold table in counts (caught, missed, false alarms) speaks the language of the people who use the model.
  • When there's a requirement, pick the highest threshold that meets it; use F1 only when there's no rule.
  • When the test result disappoints, report it. Tuning on the test set destroys your only honest number.
  • A threshold belongs to one trained model; retrain, and you choose again.

#Extend it

  • Change the requirement to "at most 20 false alarms per 600 transactions" and pick the threshold that catches the most fraud under that cap.
  • Swap LogisticRegression for RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0). Do its probabilities need a different threshold for the same recall?
  • Look up TunedThresholdClassifierCV in scikit-learn (version 1.5 or newer). It automates this search with cross-validation.

#Further reading

  • Tuning the decision threshold (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's guide to choosing cutoffs, including TunedThresholdClassifierCV.
  • Thresholds and the confusion matrix (opens in a new tab): Google's interactive version of the trade-off you just charted.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 from a confusion matrix by hand.
  • Catch a report that measured the wrong positive class.
  • Show why accuracy fails on rare classes, and what to report instead.
  • Apply your own threshold to predict_proba and read the trade-off in a confusion matrix.
  • Read a three-class confusion matrix and compare two models with precision-recall curves.
  • Choose a threshold by dollar cost on validation data, then confirm it on test data.

Metrics are easy to compute and easy to misread. Most of these exercises hide a trap, the kind that turns up in real projects and in other people's reports. Do Exercise 1 on paper before touching code: if you can do it by hand, you'll never mix up precision and recall again. Use one notebook and run the cells in order.

#Warm-up: the order of ravel()

Predict the four numbers before you run this. Remember that rows are the true class, columns are the predicted class, and positive is 1:

Pair them up: (0,0) is a true negative, (1,1) twice is two true positives, (1,0) twice is two misses, and (0,1) once is one false alarm. ravel() reads the grid row by row, which is why the order is always TN, FP, FN, TP.

#Exercise 1: By hand first

A model's confusion matrix (rows = true class, columns = predicted, positive class = 1) is:

On paper, compute accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. Then check your answers by building label arrays that produce this matrix and calling scikit-learn's functions.

Need a hint?

First name the four cells: top-left is TN, top-right FP, bottom-left FN, bottom-right TP. To rebuild labels, you need 60 true 0s (50 predicted 0, 10 predicted 1) and 40 true 1s (5 predicted 0, 35 predicted 1).

Show solution

TN = 50, FP = 10, FN = 5, TP = 35, for 100 rows in total.

  • Accuracy = (35 + 50) / 100 = 0.85
  • Precision = 35 / (35 + 10) = 0.778
  • Recall = 35 / (35 + 5) = 0.875
  • F1 = 2 × 0.778 × 0.875 / (0.778 + 0.875) = 0.824

Precision and recall share the numerator, TP. The only difference is the denominator: everything the model flagged (precision) versus everything that was really positive (recall).

#Exercise 2: Which class is positive?

In the original breast cancer labels, 0 is malignant and 1 is benign. Train DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0) on all 30 features (test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=1). Print recall with the default settings, then with pos_label=0. Which number should a doctor care about?

Need a hint?

recall_score(y_test, pred) measures recall for whichever class is labeled 1. Adding pos_label=0 measures it for class 0 instead. Same predictions, different question.

Show solution

The default reports how many healthy patients were correctly cleared, which sounds great. The number a doctor needs is malignant recall: this one-question tree misses about one cancer in five. Same predictions, very different story, all from which class counts as positive. Pass pos_label, or flip the labels as the Notes did.

#Exercise 3: The accuracy paradox

Make a dataset where only about 3% of rows are positive:

Split it (test_size=0.3, stratify=y_rare, random_state=0). For a default DummyClassifier and a default LogisticRegression, print accuracy, recall, and F1 (pass zero_division=0 to F1). Which model does accuracy say is better? Which is actually more useful?

Need a hint?

Loop over the two models, fit each on the training rows, predict the test rows, and print all three metrics on one line so the comparison is side by side.

Show solution

Accuracy calls the dummy the winner, by a hair. But the dummy never predicts positive, so its recall and F1 are 0: it has never found a single positive case. Logistic regression at least finds some. With rare classes, accuracy mostly measures how rare the class is. The logistic model's low recall also suggests lowering its threshold, which is the next exercise. Week 6 brings more tools for imbalance.

#Exercise 4: Write your own predict

Rebuild the two-feature screening model from the Notes (mean radius and mean texture, labels flipped so 1 = malignant, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0, StandardScaler plus LogisticRegression). Write predict_with_threshold(model, X, threshold). Check that it matches model.predict at 0.5, then print confusion matrices at 0.5 and 0.25. How many extra cancers does 0.25 catch, and at what price?

Need a hint?

Your function needs one line: compare column 1 of model.predict_proba(X) with the threshold, and turn the True/False result into 1/0 with .astype(int).

Show solution

Lowering the threshold to 0.25 shrinks the bottom-left cell (missed cancers) by 3 and grows the top-right cell (false alarms) by 11. Whether 3 caught cancers are worth 11 extra scans is a judgment about costs, not a math question. The final exercise makes that judgment with numbers.

#Exercise 5: Three classes

Train KNeighborsClassifier() on only the first two wine features, alcohol and malic acid (test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=0). Draw the 3×3 confusion matrix with ConfusionMatrixDisplay and print a classification report. Which class is hardest, and which pair of classes gets mixed up most?

Need a hint?

In a multi-class matrix, each class gets its own precision and recall, treating that class as positive and the other two together as negative. Look for the largest number off the diagonal.

Show solution

Class 2 is hardest, with the lowest F1. The biggest single confusion is 4 class-0 wines predicted as class 2, top right of the matrix: both classes are high in alcohol, so with only these two features they overlap. Class 1 (low alcohol) is easy. Macro avg comes out a little below weighted avg, because the weakest class is also the smallest.

#Exercise 6: Compare models before choosing a threshold

On the screening split from Exercise 4 (labels flipped, same random_state=0), compare the two-feature model with a logistic regression that uses all 30 features. Don't pick a threshold: plot both models' precision-recall curves on one chart, and print each model's average precision and ROC AUC. Which model would you deploy, and does the answer depend on which threshold you later choose?

Need a hint?

Split data.data and y2 with the same arguments to get the 30-feature version. PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(model, X_test, y_test, ax=ax, name="...") draws one curve; call it twice with the same ax. average_precision_score and roc_auc_score both take the true labels and predict_proba(X)[:, 1].

Show solution

Splitting data.data with the same test_size, stratify, and random_state puts exactly the same tumors in the test set, so both curves are scored on identical rows. The 30-feature curve sits above the other almost everywhere, and both summary numbers agree. When one curve dominates like that, the choice doesn't depend on the threshold: whatever recall you need, the bigger model gets it with fewer false alarms. If the curves crossed, the better model would depend on where you plan to operate, and you'd decide after fixing the requirement.

#Challenge: put a price on mistakes

Use the fraud data and the three-way split from the code-along. A missed fraud costs the bank $500; reviewing a false alarm costs $20 of staff time. Write total_cost(y_true, proba, threshold). Search thresholds from 0.02 to 0.98 in steps of 0.02 on the validation set, plot cost against threshold, pick the cheapest, and then report the test-set cost for the default 0.5 and for your threshold.

Need a hint?

Cost is fn * 500 + fp * 20, using the counts from confusion_matrix(...).ravel(). np.argmin(costs) gives the position of the cheapest threshold in your list. Don't touch X_test until the threshold is chosen.

Show solution

A missed fraud costs 25 times more than a review, so the cheapest threshold is low, accepting many false alarms to catch more fraud. On the untouched test set it cuts the cost roughly in half compared with 0.5. There's a neat rule of thumb behind this: if the model's probabilities were perfectly trustworthy, you'd flag whenever P(fraud) × $500 exceeds (1 − P(fraud)) × $20, which works out to a threshold of 20 / 520 ≈ 0.04. The search landed higher because real probabilities are never perfectly trustworthy, and that's exactly why you search on validation data instead of trusting the formula.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a single train/test split gives a noisy score, and how k-fold cross-validation fixes it.
  • Run cross_val_score with a shared StratifiedKFold and report the result as mean ± std.
  • Keep preprocessing inside a pipeline so every fold stays leak-free.
  • Read a validation curve to choose a hyperparameter, and a learning curve to decide whether more data would help.

Here is a decision tree trained on the breast cancer data 30 times. The model, its settings, and the data never change. The only thing that changes is random_state in train_test_split, which decides which 25% of tumors land in the test set. Before you run it, guess how far apart the best and worst test accuracy will be.

Eleven points separate the luckiest split from the unluckiest one. If you had run this once and written "my tree is 86% accurate," you'd be reporting the split, not the model. A single test score is one draw from that histogram. This week is about drawing several on purpose and reporting what they say together.

#Let every row take a turn as the test

Here's the intuition. Instead of one exam, give the model five, and make sure no question is ever on two of them. Each exam is graded by a model that never studied those questions. The average tells you how good the model is; the spread tells you how much to trust the average.

Now precisely. k-fold cross-validation cuts the rows into k equal parts called folds. In round 1 the model trains on folds 2 to k and is scored on fold 1. In round 2 it trains on everything except fold 2 and is scored on fold 2, and so on. After k rounds, every row has been used for validation exactly once and for training k − 1 times, and you have k scores.

For classifiers, use StratifiedKFold, which keeps the class mix roughly the same in every fold, and turn on shuffle=True. Let's look at what it actually hands back:

cv.split yields pairs of index arrays, one pair per round. Notice the last number on each line: every validation fold is 62% to 63% benign, matching the full dataset's 62.7%, because the splitter is stratified. Shuffling is why the dark rows are scattered rather than five solid blocks.

You'll rarely loop over cv.split yourself. cross_val_score does the fitting and scoring for you:

Report the mean as your estimate and the standard deviation as its wobble: "about 0.97, give or take 0.02." The fold scores run from 0.947 to 0.991, so a single unlucky split could have reported either end.

Two details in that cell matter more than they look:

  • The pipeline goes in, not a pre-scaled X. cross_val_score refits the whole pipeline in each round, so the scaler learns its means only from that round's training rows. Scale X first and every validation fold has already shaped the scaler.
  • cv is an object you keep. Pass the same cv to every model you try and they're all graded on identical folds. That's what makes next week's comparisons fair.

Cross-validation doesn't replace the test set. You use CV to make choices, and because you made choices with it, its scores end up slightly flattering. The untouched test set is the final, unbiased check.

#Overfitting and underfitting on a validation curve

A model underfits when it's too simple for the pattern: think of a student who learned one rule and applies it to everything. Training and validation scores are both low. A model overfits when it memorizes the training rows, quirks included, like a student who memorized last year's answer key. Training is high, validation is noticeably lower, and that gap is the warning sign.

A tree's max_depth is a dial from "one rule" to "memorize everything." validation_curve cross-validates the model once per dial setting and returns train and validation scores, each shaped (settings, folds):

.mean(axis=1) averages across the five folds for each depth, and the shaded band is ±1 std of the validation scores. Read it left to right. At depth 1 both lines are lowest: underfitting. The validation line peaks at depths 4 and 5 (0.928) and then sags, while training keeps climbing to a perfect 1.000. Every extra level after the peak is spent memorizing. Pick the setting at the validation peak, and if a few settings are within the shaded band of each other, prefer the simplest.

#Learning curves: would more data help?

A validation curve changes the model. A learning curve keeps the model fixed and changes how many training rows it gets. It answers a question that can save you weeks: should you collect more data, or change the model?

The two panels are the two classic shapes:

  • Left, high variance. The deep tree scores 1.000 on its own rows at every size. Validation climbs as rows are added, but a wide gap remains. More data would help a bit; a simpler or averaged model (a random forest, next week) would help more.
  • Right, high bias. The stump's two lines settle a few points apart after about 150 rows and stop moving, and even its training score is stuck near 0.93. Doubling the data won't help, because one split can't express a better rule. The fix is a more flexible model or better features.

The good shape is the third one: both lines high and close together.

⚠️ Watch out

Three mistakes that make cross-validation lie.

  1. Preprocessing outside the pipeline. StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) before cross_val_score lets every validation fold leak into the scaler. Put every step in the pipeline you pass in.
  2. Reporting the best fold. The best of five is luck; report the mean and the std.
  3. Choosing a setting by training score. The training line on a validation curve always rewards the most complex model. Choose by validation.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1On the same five folds, model A scores 0.951 ± 0.020 and model B scores 0.957 ± 0.025. What's the most defensible conclusion?

  • A 0.006 gap is far smaller than either model's fold-to-fold wobble, so the means alone can't separate them.

  • Because the folds are shared, you can check how many folds each model wins. If it's 3 to 2, nobody is ahead.

  • A slightly smaller std means slightly steadier scores, not better ones. With a lower mean, that's not a win.

Show answer

B. Because the folds are shared, you can check how many folds each model wins. If it's 3 to 2, nobody is ahead.

2A learning curve shows training accuracy fixed at 1.00 while validation climbs from 0.80 to 0.90 and is still rising at the largest size. What's the most promising next step?

  • The model is already memorizing its training rows. More flexibility would widen the gap.

  • A big gap with validation still rising is high variance. More rows or a simpler, regularized model both attack it.

  • Rising at the right edge means it hasn't finished improving, and the gap says it's overfitting.

Show answer

B. A big gap with validation still rising is high variance. More rows or a simpler, regularized model both attack it.

3Your notebook runs X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) and then cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_scaled, y, cv=cv). What's wrong?

  • It doesn't use labels, but it does use every row's feature values, including the rows that will be validation folds.

  • Put the scaler in a pipeline and pass the pipeline, so each round fits the scaler on its training rows only.

  • It runs without complaint, which is exactly why this leak is easy to miss.

Show answer

B. Put the scaler in a pipeline and pass the pipeline, so each round fits the scaler on its training rows only.

4The validation curve above gives depth 3 → 0.917, depth 4 → 0.928, depth 5 → 0.928, depth 8 → 0.916, with validation std around 0.02. Which depth would you choose?

  • Training fit is not the goal. Depth 8 is more complex and scores lower on validation.

  • Depths 3 to 5 are within one std of each other, so take the simplest tree near the peak. It's easier to explain and usually steadier on new data.

  • Choosing with the test set turns it into a second validation set, and then no unbiased score is left.

Show answer

B. Depths 3 to 5 are within one std of each other, so take the simplest tree near the peak. It's easier to explain and usually steadier on new data.

Key takeaways

  • One train/test split is one draw from a wide distribution. Cross-validation takes k draws and reports mean ± std.
  • Use StratifiedKFold(shuffle=True, random_state=...) for classifiers, make it once, and reuse it everywhere.
  • Pass the whole pipeline to cross_val_score, validation_curve, and learning_curve so preprocessing is refit inside every fold.
  • On a validation curve, choose by the validation line and prefer the simplest setting near its peak.
  • A learning curve with a big, shrinking gap says variance (more data or a simpler model); two low lines that meet say bias (a more flexible model).
  • Cross-validation is for choosing. The test set is still scored once, at the end.

  • scikit-learn User Guide: Validation curves and learning curves (opens in a new tab) has the official explanations and display helpers for both plots.
  • scikit-learn example: Visualizing cross-validation behavior (opens in a new tab) draws the folds of many splitters side by side, a good way to see what "stratified" and "grouped" really do.
